The second fact, oracleCalls = 0, certifies that the emitted list contains no opaque oracle instruction, every instruction is a concrete primitive gate (X, RY, RZ, or CX). It therefore certifies that this particular witness has been fully synthesized down to primitives with nothing left abstract. It does NOT certify that an arbitrary-width banded access oracle can be synthesized to zero oracle calls; the witness is deliberately a fixed three-bit instance. Importing a block-encoding theory module only brings definitions and earlier lemmas into scope; module imports never entail theorem claims, so importing a theory that mentions oracles is not a claim that any oracle was realized. reference_answer: The projection formula implements the clean PREPARE bra acting on the left of an operator. Reading it register by register: the coefficient component is pinned to the clean reference value c0 on the right-factor input, because the bra lives in the clean coefficient sector; the system component is pinned to the fixed clean system row, because the bra does not touch the system; and the selector component is NOT pinned, it is summed over all selector values s. Each selector term is weighted by conj(PREPARE[s, s0]), the complex conjugate of the amplitude that PREPARE assigns to selector s when started from the clean selector reference s0. This conjugate weight is correct because projecting with a bra <psi| contributes the conjugate of the ket amplitudes: the clean bra is the row of the conjugate transpose of PREPARE indexed by s0, whose entry in column s is exactly conj(PREPARE[s, s0]). The important semantic point is coherence: the selector sum is a coherent superposition, not a classical mixture. The terms conj(PREPARE[s,s0]) * (right factor at selector s) are added as complex amplitudes before any modulus is taken, so cross-selector interference is possible; different selector branches can reinforce or cancel. An incoherent classical mixture would instead add nonnegative probabilities |PREPARE[s,s0]|^2 weighting each branch's outcome independently, with no interference. The prepare/unprepare structure of the full block is precisely what converts this coherent selector sum into the intended weighted combination of amplitude blocks, which an incoherent mixture could not reproduce.

question: Any complex square matrix A splits as A = H1 + i H2 where H1 = (A + A-dagger)/2 and H2 = (A - A-dagger)/(2i). Prove that H1 and H2 are both Hermitian (equal to their own conjugate transpose entrywise) and that H1 + i H2 reconstructs A, taking care with the factor of i in the denominator of H2. Explain why this is the matrix analogue of writing a complex number as real part plus i times imaginary part.
reference_answer: Work entrywise with the conjugate-transpose convention A-dagger[i,j] = conj(A[j,i]). Define H1[i,j] = (A[i,j] + conj(A[j,i]))/2 and H2[i,j] = (A[i,j] - conj(A[j,i]))/(2i). Hermiticity of H1: its (j,i) conjugate is conj(H1[j,i]) = conj((A[j,i] + conj(A[i,j]))/2) = (conj(A[j,i]) + A[i,j])/2 = H1[i,j], using that conjugation is additive, fixes 1/2, and is involutive. So H1[i,j] = conj(H1[j,i]), i.e. H1 is Hermitian. Hermiticity of H2: conj(H2[j,i]) = conj((A[j,i] - conj(A[i,j]))/(2i)) = (conj(A[j,i]) - A[i,j])/(conj(2i)) = (conj(A[j,i]) - A[i,j])/(-2i) = (A[i,j] - conj(A[j,i]))/(2i) = H2[i,j], where conj(2i) = -2i and dividing the negated numerator by the negated denominator restores the sign; one uses 2i != 0. So H2 is Hermitian. Reconstruction: H1[i,j] + i*H2[i,j] = (A[i,j] + conj(A[j,i]))/2 + i*(A[i,j] - conj(A[j,i]))/(2i). The i cancels the i in the denominator of the second term (again 2i != 0), giving (A[i,j] + conj(A[j,i]))/2 + (A[i,j] - conj(A[j,i]))/2 = A[i,j]. So A = H1 + i H2. This is the exact matrix analogue of z = Re(z) + i Im(z): the Hermitian part plays the role of the real part (fixed by conjugate transpose, as the real part is fixed by conjugation) and H2 plays the role of the imaginary part (made Hermitian by dividing by 2i), and the two together rebuild A just as real and imaginary parts rebuild a scalar.

question: A homogenization step embeds a problem matrix A and an inhomogeneous block B into the direct-sum matrix S = [[A, B], [0, 0]] on the doubled index set. One then forms its Hermitian part S1 = (S + S-dagger)/2. Prove that the lower-right block of S1 is identically zero, and show that the lower-left block of S1 equals B/2 PROVIDED B is Hermitian, while without that hypothesis the lower-left block is instead B-dagger/2. reference_answer: Write S on the index set that is the disjoint union of two copies of the base, with blocks indexed by (left,left),(left,right),(right,left),(right,right). By definition S has upper-left A, upper-right B, and both lower blocks 0. The Hermitian part is S1[r,c] = (S[r,c] + conj(S[c,r]))/2 entrywise. Lower-right block: for right-indices i,j, S1[(right i),(right j)] = (S[(right i),(right j)] + conj(S[(right j),(right i)]))/2 = (0 + conj(0))/2 = 0, so the whole lower-right block vanishes identically with no hypothesis. Upper-right block: for left-row i, right-column j, S1[(left i),(right j)] = (S[(left i),(right j)] + conj(S[(right j),(left i)]))/2 = (B[i,j] + conj(0))/2 = B[i,j]/2; the second term vanishes because the lower-left block of S is 0, so no hypothesis on B is needed. Lower-left block: for right-row i, left-column j, S1[(right i),(left j)] = (S[(right i),(left j)] + conj(S[(left j),(right i)]))/2 = (0 + conj(B[j,i]))/2 = conj(B[j,i])/2 = B-dagger[i,j]/2. This equals B[i,j]/2 exactly when B-dagger = B, i.e. when B is Hermitian; the hypothesis is used precisely to rewrite conj(B[j,i]) as B[i,j]. Without Hermiticity the honest value is B-dagger/2, which can differ from B/2. The asymmetry is structural: the upper-right block reads B directly from S and its conjugate partner is a zero block, so no hypothesis is needed; the lower-left block reads a zero from S and sees B only through the conjugate of the upper-right partner, so it inevitably sees B-dagger and needs Hermiticity to be reported as B.

reference_answer: Each controlled-phase source piece contributes, on the lower-right (right,right) block, the diagonal value N_A * e^{i phi} where phi is that piece's filler phase; the two pieces (one carrying A, one carrying A-dagger) are averaged with weight 1/2 each, and a third Pauli-X-tensor-B piece contributes nothing to the lower-right block. With both printed phases equal to pi, e^{i pi} = -1, so the lower-right clean entry is (1/2)(N_A * (-1)) + (1/2)(N_A * (-1)) = -N_A. Since the intended S1 has lower-right block identically 0, equality of the printed construction with S1 would force -N_A = 0, i.e. N_A = 0. Contrapositively, whenever N_A is nonzero the printed all-(-1) phase choice does NOT equal S1: it is off by a nonzero constant filler on the lower-right. The corrected assignment keeps one piece's filler phase at pi (value -1) but sets the OTHER piece's filler phase to 0 (value e^{i*0} = +1). Then the lower-right clean entry becomes (1/2)(N_A * (+1)) + (1/2)(N_A * (-1)) = (1/2)N_A - (1/2)N_A = 0, cancelling the filler. Crucially this phase change touches only the lower-right filler diagonal; the selected upper-left A block, the A-dagger contribution and the upper-right B/2 block are unaffected, so the corrected construction reproduces exactly S1 (under Hermitian B). The lesson is that two equal filler phases ADD on the irrelevant block instead of cancelling, and that a filler which is harmless on the clean sector only when it cancels must be verified, not assumed, when composing phased oracle pieces.

The second term vanishes because <0|1> = 0. The first term is A_jj <i|j> = A_jj delta_ij. When i = j this equals A_jj = A_ii; when i != j it is 0. Hence <0|<i| U_A |0>|j> = A_ii delta_ij, which is precisely the (i,j) entry of the diagonal matrix A. By the definition of block encoding, (<0| tensor I) U_A (|0> tensor I) = A exactly, with one ancilla qubit (m = 1) and subnormalization alpha = 1, so U_A is in BE_{1,1}(A). No permutation oracle is needed because for a DIAGONAL matrix the row index equals the column index: the single nonzero entry in column j sits at row c(j) = j, i.e. the sparsity permutation c is the identity. In the general 1-sparse case the unique nonzero entry of column j lives at row c(j) != j, so one must apply an index permutation O_c |j> = |c(j)> to move the amplitude-carrying basis state from |j> to |c(j)>; for the diagonal case c = id, so O_c = I and U_A = O_A alone suffices. A basis of the antisymmetric subspace is given by the wedges of distinct basis vectors, one for each unordered pair of distinct indices, of which there are d choose two equal to d times d minus one over two. These dimensions sum to d squared, the dimension of the full second tensor power, confirming the direct sum.

question: A Werner state is entangled if and only if its visibility, the trace against the swap operator, is negative. Prove the entangled direction using the positive-partial-transpose criterion by computing the partial transpose of the swap operator and locating a negative eigenvalue, and explain why nonnegative visibility yields a separable state.

Partial transpose of the swap: writing the swap in a product basis as the sum over index pairs of the outer product that exchanges the two labels, transposing on the second subsystem turns it into the sum over index pairs of the outer product of a maximally correlated vector, which equals d times the projector onto the maximally entangled state. The identity is unchanged by partial transposition. Hence the partial transpose of the Werner state is an affine combination of the identity and the maximally entangled projector; this operator has two eigenvalues, one on the maximally entangled vector and one on its orthogonal complement. A short computation shows the eigenvalue associated with the maximally entangled direction is proportional to the visibility times the quantity d squared minus one, which is negative exactly when the visibility is negative (using d at least two). A state whose partial transpose has a negative eigenvalue fails the positive-partial-transpose criterion and is therefore entangled; thus negative visibility forces entanglement. Conversely, for nonnegative visibility one exhibits an explicit separable preparation: twirling a suitable product state produces a Werner state of any prescribed nonnegative visibility, and twirling preserves separability because it averages conjugates of a separable state; hence every Werner state with nonnegative visibility is separable. Combining the two directions gives the stated equivalence.

question: A multipartite state on n copies of C^d that is invariant under the simultaneous action of the same unitary on every copy must be a linear combination of the permutation operators of the symmetric group acting on the factors. Prove this using the mutual-commutant relationship between the diagonal unitary action and the factor-permutation action.
reference_answer: Let A be the algebra spanned by the diagonal unitary operators that apply the same unitary to all n factors, and let B be the algebra spanned by the factor permutations. By the Schur-Weyl mutual-commutant theorem these two algebras are each other's commutants inside the full operator algebra of the tensor power: the commutant of the diagonal unitary algebra is exactly the span of the factor permutations. The invariance hypothesis states that conjugating the state by every diagonal unitary leaves it fixed, which is equivalent to the state commuting with every diagonal unitary (conjugation invariance for unitaries is the same as commuting with them). Therefore the state lies in the commutant of the diagonal unitary algebra. By the mutual-commutant theorem that commutant is the span of the factor permutations, so the state is a linear combination of the permutation operators, as claimed. The remark that these permutation operators are not in general positive semidefinite shows this expansion, while always valid, need not display the state as a manifestly valid density operator; that is a separate positivity question, not an obstruction to the linear-combination conclusion.

Suppose U block-encodes A with normalizer alpha (so the auxiliary-zero projected block equals A/alpha) and the input system state is a normalized vector v. Because the auxiliary-zero projected block of U equals A/alpha, w_clean = (A/alpha) v. The all-zero postselection keeps exactly the clean branch, so the unnormalized clean output is (A/alpha) v with squared norm ||(A/alpha) v||^2 = ||A v||^2 / alpha^2, and the post-measurement normalized state is (A v)/||A v||. The success probability of the all-zero auxiliary outcome is therefore p = ||A v||^2 / alpha^2 = (||A v|| / alpha)^2. This equals (||A v||/alpha)^2 exactly whenever the projected block is exactly A/alpha (the exact block-encoding case); in the epsilon-approximate case it is this value up to an O(epsilon) correction. Since U is unitary, the total output norm is 1, so p <= 1 with equality only in the degenerate case ||A v|| = alpha (e.g. alpha = ||A|| and v a top singular vector with the orthogonal branch empty); generically ||A v|| < alpha (alpha is chosen at least the operator norm so the encoding is valid for all v), so p < 1 strictly. The cost implication: one query to U succeeds with probability p that can be far below 1, so naive repetition costs O(1/p) = O(alpha^2/||A v||^2) trials; amplitude amplification reduces this to O(alpha/||A v||) queries. This 1/alpha success penalty is exactly why the normalizer alpha is a charged resource and why alpha should be kept close to ||A||.

By the block structure the component in the all-zeros ancilla sector is |0...0> (A/alpha)|b>, and the rest is orthogonal to the all-zeros ancilla subspace. The probability of measuring the ancillas in all-zeros is the squared norm of that component: p(0) = ||(A/alpha)|b>||^2 = (1/alpha^2) <b| A-dagger A |b> = ||A|b>||^2 / alpha^2. Consequence 1 (norm recovery): the norm that is 'lost' when the output is renormalized is encoded in the success probability, since ||A|b>|| = alpha sqrt(p(0)); measuring p(0) (by repetition) therefore recovers ||A|b>||. question: When a matrix A is embedded (up to a positive factor alpha) as the all-zeros block of a larger unitary, so that A/alpha is a submatrix of a unitary, prove the necessary scaling constraint on alpha. First prove the auxiliary fact that any submatrix block of a unitary has operator norm at most 1. Deduce the sharp lower bound alpha must satisfy in terms of the operator norm of A, explain why an exact unit-factor embedding is impossible when A has operator norm bigger than 1, and state what role alpha then plays and whether the bound alone guarantees an efficiently implementable embedding.
reference_answer: Submatrix-norm fact: let U be unitary and let B = P U Q be a block, where P and Q are projectors onto the output and input index sets of the block (equivalently B = <0^m| U |0^m> as an operator on the system register). For any unit input vector v (extended by zeros outside the block), ||B v|| = ||P U (Q v)|| <= ||U (Q v)|| = ||Q v|| <= ||v|| = 1, since projectors are norm-nonincreasing and U is norm-preserving. Taking the supremum over unit v gives ||B|| <= 1. Lower bound on alpha: if A/alpha is such a block of a unitary, then ||A/alpha|| <= 1, i.e. ||A|| <= alpha, so alpha >= ||A|| is necessary. In particular if ||A|| > 1 there is no exact embedding with alpha = 1 (a unit-factor block would force ||A|| <= 1); one must take alpha >= ||A|| > 1. Role of alpha: it rescales A so that A/alpha fits inside a unitary as a contraction, at the cost of a success probability that falls like 1/alpha^2; the smallest admissible alpha is the operator norm ||A|| (achieved by a singular-value dilation). Finally, the inequality alpha >= ||A|| is only a necessary existence condition on the scale: it does not by itself provide a circuit, since constructing a unitary whose block is A/alpha and that is implementable with few elementary gates requires further structure or oracle access to A; the bound guarantees feasibility of the scale, not efficiency of implementation.

question: A target operator is written as a linear combination T = sum_i alpha_i U_i of unitaries U_i, and is implemented by a prepare-select-unprepare scheme in which each coefficient is split as alpha_i = beta_i gamma_i, a left preparation loads the vector of beta_i (normalized by the 2-norm of beta), a controlled selection applies U_i, and a right unpreparation loads the vector of gamma_i. The resulting construction embeds T with subnormalization factor equal to the product of the 2-norms of the beta and gamma vectors. Prove, using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, that this subnormalization factor is at least the 1-norm of the coefficient vector alpha, and determine the splitting beta_i, gamma_i that makes the factor equal to that 1-norm. Explain why this is the best (smallest) achievable factor for this scheme and hence the most favorable success probability.
reference_answer: The scheme produces subnormalization factor ||beta||_2 ||gamma||_2 where ||beta||_2 = sqrt(sum_i |beta_i|^2) and likewise for gamma. Since alpha_i = beta_i gamma_i, the 1-norm of alpha is ||alpha||_1 = sum_i |alpha_i| = sum_i |beta_i| |gamma_i|. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to the vectors (|beta_i|)_i and (|gamma_i|)_i, sum_i |beta_i| |gamma_i| <= sqrt(sum_i |beta_i|^2) sqrt(sum_i |gamma_i|^2) = ||beta||_2 ||gamma||_2. Therefore ||alpha||_1 <= ||beta||_2 ||gamma||_2, i.e. the subnormalization factor is at least ||alpha||_1 for every admissible split. Equality in Cauchy-Schwarz holds iff the vectors (|beta_i|) and (|gamma_i|) are proportional; combined with |beta_i gamma_i| = |alpha_i|, the symmetric optimum is |beta_i| = |gamma_i| = sqrt(|alpha_i|) for every i. With that choice ||beta||_2^2 = ||gamma||_2^2 = sum_i |alpha_i| = ||alpha||_1, so ||beta||_2 ||gamma||_2 = ||alpha||_1, attaining the lower bound. Since the success probability of keeping the all-zeros ancilla scales inversely with the square of the subnormalization factor, minimizing it to ||alpha||_1 maximizes the success probability for this prepare-select-unprepare implementation; no split in this scheme can do better, because ||alpha||_1 is a hard lower bound from Cauchy-Schwarz. (When all alpha_i >= 0 this optimal choice also makes the unpreparation the adjoint of the preparation.)

Characterize the active (reduced) bond dimensions it produces: give the backward recurrence the reduced left rank of each core obeys, prove the two-sided bound on the head rank of any nonempty canonicalized train, and derive the sharp consequence that the penultimate active bond of a scalar-to-scalar train (one core, both boundaries dimension one) has dimension at most two. reference_answer: Right-canonicalization reduces each core by a thin factorization whose Q-factor row count is min(l, 2*m'), where l is the current left dimension and m' is the already-reduced next bond. So the reduced left rank obeys the backward min recurrence l' = min(l, 2*m') computed from the terminal bond inward. Two-sided head bound: for any nonempty canonicalized train D = cons Q tail with reduced head l', from l' = min(l, 2*m') we get both l' <= l (the min is at most its first argument) and l' <= 2*m' (the min is at most its second argument), where m' is the next active bond. Thus the head rank is bounded by the original left dimension and by twice the next active rank simultaneously. Sharp scalar case: for a one-core chain with both boundaries dimension one (Chain 1 l 1), the tail is the empty chain whose only bond is the terminal bond of dimension one, so m' = 1. The head bound l' <= 2*m' becomes l' <= 2. This is sharp: a core emitting one bit from a scalar boundary can legitimately populate both values of that bit, so the reduced bond genuinely reaches dimension two. No enlargement: the maximal bond of D is bounded by that of the original chain, because each reduced left rank min(l, 2*m') is at most l and, inductively, the tail's maximal bond does not grow; taking the max over cores preserves the inequality. Hence canonicalization is a non-expanding rank reduction with an explicit min recurrence and a tight penultimate-bond-at-most-two corollary.

(ii) The sharp first-column theorem that recovers f(b)/sqrt(normSq f) for every entry is stated with a STRICT positivity hypothesis on the entries, yet the construction clearly tolerates many exact zeros internally. reference_answer: (i) A zero sibling pair (a = b = 0) means the entire subtree hanging below that split carries no amplitude: the marginal mass at that prefix is zero, so there is nothing to rotate between the two children. The rotation angle multiplies a zero marginal in the first-column recursion, so any angle would give the same (zero) contribution; assigning angle zero is the canonical, well-defined choice and avoids an undefined polar angle (a/0). The split-level identity still holds exactly at a zero pair because both children are forced to zero and the rotation applied to a zero norm yields zero. So interior zeros that occur as whole vanishing subtrees are harmless: the marginal recursion and the per-split identity both pass through them. (ii) The strict positivity hypothesis in the sharp flat theorem is NOT needed for the circuit to be unitary or for the general first-column recursion, which only needs the global norm to be positive (so sqrt(normSq f) is nonzero and the normalized target f(b)/sqrt(normSq f) is well defined).
